title: Climate adaptation is being framed as a labour-market conversion problem: resilience investment can offset job losses only through sectoral reallocation and worker protection
source_unit: World Bank, Jobs in a Changing Climate: Insights from Country Climate and Development Reports covering 93 economies
geography: Low- and middle-income economies; 93 Country Climate and Development Reports representing 64 percent of the population and 77 percent of GDP of low- and middle-income countries

observations.period: 2050 horizon; climate-related employment exposure in 49 analyzed countries

denominator.unit: countries with quantified employment effects in the report's analyzed set

potential_job_losses.unit: job-equivalents potentially lost by 2050 across 49 countries

global_extrapolation.unit: job-equivalents when the 49-country estimate is extrapolated across all low- and middle-income countries

employment_mechanism.value: climate impacts can negatively affect employment through sectoral, regional, and economic changes

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of Country Climate and Development Reports with modelled employment implications; the global figure is an extrapolation, not a forecast of realized individual job losses.
observations.uncertainty: Country coverage, model assumptions, climate scenarios, sector definitions, time horizon, and extrapolation make the figures unsuitable for direct country-by-country or worker-level interpretation.
observations.subgroup: Workers in climate-exposed sectors and regions, low-income households, informal workers, women, youth, firms, communities, and countries with limited adaptation finance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Climate change can create as well as destroy work; aggregate job counts may hide wage, safety, quality, location, and access losses, and adaptation can protect assets without protecting the same workers.

observations.period: 2050 horizon; adaptation investment and employment opportunity in 49 analyzed countries

denominator.unit: countries in the quantified adaptation-job analysis

adaptation_jobs.unit: equivalent more and better-paid jobs estimated across the 49 countries

global_extrapolation.unit: equivalent jobs when adaptation effects are extrapolated globally

job_quality.value: the report frames adaptation investment as capable of creating more and better-paid jobs while protecting vulnerable workers and communities

conversion_condition.value: resilience investment must be connected to human capital, business conditions, worker reallocation, and protection

observations.method: World Bank synthesis and model-based estimate of adaptation-related employment benefits, including a global extrapolation.
observations.uncertainty: The estimate is not a count of announced jobs, filled jobs, wage gains, or net household welfare; “equivalent jobs” and “better-paid” depend on modelling and sectoral assumptions.
observations.subgroup: Workers transitioning into adaptation sectors, firms investing in resilience, communities receiving infrastructure, low-income households, and workers requiring reskilling or relocation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Adaptation projects can be capital-intensive, temporary, or captured by skilled workers and firms; new jobs may not be accessible to those losing work or living far from investment.

observations.period: 2026; cross-country evidence base and development coverage

denominator.unit: economies represented by Country Climate and Development Reports in the synthesis

population_coverage.unit: percent of low- and middle-income-country population represented

gdp_coverage.unit: percent of low- and middle-income-country GDP represented

policy_scope.value: the reports connect climate and development goals to job creation, economic growth, resilience, and nationally determined contributions

observations.method: Cross-report synthesis of 93 World Bank Country Climate and Development Reports.
observations.uncertainty: Coverage is broad but not universal; represented population and GDP do not guarantee comparable country methods, labour-market data, climate assumptions, or distributional measurement.
observations.subgroup: National governments, local authorities, workers, firms, sectors, regions, households, development-finance institutions, and communities making adaptation choices.
observations.counterinterpretation: A large report portfolio can produce strategic coherence while still leaving implementation fragmented, finance-constrained, or politically contested at country and local levels.

observations.period: 2050 horizon; low-emission development and sectoral transition

denominator.unit: low-emission development and labour-market transition pathway

short_term_direction.value: low-emission development can deliver net economic gains over the short term in most countries

aggregate_employment.value: aggregate employment effects may be modest while sectoral and regional shifts are significant

creation_and_decline.value: emerging technologies and industries may create opportunities while other sectors decline

policy_requirements.value: human capital, business conditions, worker reallocation, and protection of vulnerable people and communities are identified as policy requirements

observations.method: World Bank comparative climate-development synthesis distinguishing aggregate employment from sectoral and regional reallocation.
observations.uncertainty: Modelled aggregate gains do not show who transitions, who pays adjustment costs, whether jobs are decent, or how political conflict over pace and place will be resolved.
observations.subgroup: Workers in declining and emerging sectors, firms, regions dependent on carbon-intensive activity, young people entering work, and households facing energy or mobility costs.
observations.counterinterpretation: A positive aggregate transition can coexist with concentrated regional decline, skill mismatch, wage loss, stranded communities, and political backlash if redistribution and voice are weak.

related_sources.claim: World Bank Country Climate and Development Reports as the underlying country evidence base.
World Bank publication landing page for the report, where available.

boundary: This record adds a climate-to-work conversion route linking adaptation, low-emission development, sectoral reallocation, human capital, business investment, vulnerable households, and geopolitical/development finance. The job figures are modelled estimates and extrapolations from a 49-country quantified set and 93 CCDRs; they are not realized job counts, worker-level forecasts, wage evidence, or proof that adaptation benefits are distributed fairly.
